title: Story close: the little way is yours
hookLine: an elevator instead of a staircase: is the little way gentle news, or the hardest road of all?
tomorrow: what can a bare winter tree teach a young man?

cards: Productivity apps promise the hack: the one trick, the five-minute routine, the shortcut to the top. Thérèse lived in an age of inventions too, and she noticed one.
In Manuscript C she writes that the rich no longer had to climb their stairs; they had elevators. Holiness, to her, looked like a rough staircase, and she was too small to climb it.
So she went looking in scripture for an elevator. What she found, readers still argue about.

teach.b: She found it in two verses. Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." And Isaiah, where God says: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you."
The elevator, she decides, is Jesus's arms. To be lifted, she doesn't need to grow up. She needs to stay little.
That's the little way: small things, great love, trust like a child. Readers take it two ways.
One side says: this is gentle news. No heroics, no ladder of achievements. Anyone, tired or ordinary or failing, can walk it today, and that's why people love her.
The other side says: don't be fooled by the word little. Remember the petals: not letting a single small sacrifice slip by. A smile for the one who grates, every day.
That's harder than one big gesture, because it never stops. Both sides can point to her pages. Maybe both are right: the work is small and constant, and the lifting isn't hers.

That's the whole story, twenty days of it: a notebook written under obedience, every flower, a mother lost, Mary's smile, a Christmas, a condemned man, a pope, the convent door, a covered face, the splash, the petals, two brothers, and her last plain words.
None of it was little to her.

how: Catholics who love Thérèse often describe her little way as doing ordinary things with great love and trusting God like a child, and they read The Story of a Soul as its handbook.

s: the little way means doing nothing and letting God do it all
she never lets a small sacrifice slip by; the lifting is God's, the small acts are hers.
her picture for the little way is an elevator
she was too small for the stairs; the elevator is Jesus's arms.
Thérèse said she had to grow up spiritually to be lifted
she says she must stay little, and become even more so.

games.q: your friend wants to get serious about faith with a brutal thirty-day challenge. you've been reading Thérèse. what's the best case for her little way here?
o: start with small daily acts done with love, leaning on trust, not strength.
skip the effort: the little way means God does it, so nothing's needed.
go with the challenge: small things are only for beginners.
games.why: Thérèse's way is small, constant and carried by trust. readers argue whether it's gentle or demanding, but nobody reads it as doing nothing.

practice: Name three small things you'll do tomorrow with love: one at home, one at work or school, one for someone who won't know. Attach a face to each. Then let the sit carry all three.

wordCard.voice: Story close. Twenty days of Thérèse, ending where she did: small things, great love, trust like a child.

orig.note: Latin for a little one, the word for a child in the Vulgate's 'little one, let him come to me'.

carryVoice: Remember this: the little way, open to anyone, no staircase to climb first. Until next time.
